question.value: Can a dusty disk wind explain why the disk around RY Tau is hidden in optical (I band) scattered light but visible in the near-infrared (H band), and what are the grain size, dust mass, and launching region of this wind?

evidence.quote: We aim to test the hypothesis that a dusty disk wind could be responsible for the optical effect in which the disk around RY Tau is hidden in the I band, but visible in the H band.
We also want to constrain the grain size and dust mass in the wind and the wind-launching region.
The ALMA observations were taken in ALMA Band 6 ($\lambda_{c}=1.3$ mm) and were published in (cite: 2018ApJ...869...17L).

analysis_steps.goal: Measure the position angles of the scattered light horns in I and H bands

method.value: Divide images into 4-pixel-thick radial annuli outside the coronagraph, rotate image in 1 deg steps (up to 90 deg for ZIMPOL, 65 deg for IRDIS) to maximize the 4-pixel sum, refine in 0.1 deg steps within +/-10 deg for the brightest pixel out to SNR = 3, and average across annuli

evidence.quote: Therefore, annuli of a thickness of four pixels were created with increasing radius starting outside of the radius of the coronograph.
The procedure was then refined to an angle of $\pm 10^{\circ}$ around the found directions for each horn, and this time the rotation was only 0.1$^{\circ}$, but now seeking the brightest pixel.
The final angle of the horn was found by averaging the angles found for the brightest pixels per annul.

key_parameters.value: 4-pixel radial annuli, SNR >= 3 threshold, rotation limits 90 deg (ZIMPOL) and 65 deg (IRDIS, excluding inner 15 pixels of disk signal)

evidence.quote: Measurements were done starting from the edge of the coronograph to the distance from the star when the pixel intensity dropped below a signal-to-noise ratio of three compared to the background, considering this radius to be the end of the horn.
We therefore lowered the upper limit of rotation to 65$^{\circ}$ in each direction, and in this way excluded the inner 15 pixels of the signal from the disk.

findings_qualitative.value: In the SPHERE/IRDIS H-band image, the top side of the disk surface is clearly visible and separated from the two horn-like features by two dark wedges, whereas in the SPHERE/ZIMPOL I-band image only the two horns are visible and the disk is hidden.

evidence.quote: In the H band image (Fig. 1, middle panel), on the other hand, the top side, [1], of the disk surface is clearly visible, which is consistent with the sub-millimetre observation.
Two dark wedges separate the disk from the horns, one in the north [5] and one in the south-east [6].

findings_qualitative.value: A simple two-component dusty disk wind model with sub-micron to micron-sized grains (<= 1 um) elevated above the disk reproduces both the horn morphology and the shadowing of the disk in the I' band while allowing H-band photons to scatter off the disk.

evidence.quote: A model geometrically reminiscent of a dusty disk wind with small micron to sub-micron-sized grains elevated above the disk can reproduce the optical effect seen in the observations.

findings_qualitative.value: A magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) disk wind is favoured over a photo-evaporative (PE) wind and an infalling protostellar envelope because of the dark wedges separating the horns from the disk, the symmetry of the horns, the small (~10 AU) mm cavity, the presence of inner disk dust, the active jet, and the agreement of the derived mass-loss rate with MHD wind expectations.

evidence.quote: The close to symmetric horn structure in the observations of RY Tau, the opening angle and the presence of the dark wedges between the disk and the horns, all become strong indicators that the material observed above the disk is launched from the disk, rather than material falling onto the disk.
We therefore find it more likely that the wind-launching mechanism in this case is magneto-centrifugally driven.

claims.hypothesis: A dusty disk wind with small elevated grains can explain why the disk around RY Tau is hidden in the I band but visible in the H band, while producing the two horn-like scattered light features.
claims.experiment: Combined new SPHERE/IRDIS H-band polarimetric imaging with archival SPHERE/ZIMPOL I'-band and ALMA 1.3 mm images, and constructed a 2-component disk wind + multi-zone disk model in the Monte Carlo radiative transfer code MCMax3D.
claims.result: A wind-foot component (0.21-30 AU) and wind-top component (10-100 AU) containing 0.01-1 um grains and wind-foot dust mass 1e-9 M_sun <= M <= 5e-8 M_sun hides the disk in I' band above 1e-8 M_sun while keeping the disk visible in H band below 5e-8 M_sun and reproducing the two horns.
claims.finding: Small micron to sub-micron dust grains elevated above the disk in a disk wind geometry can prevent optical stellar photons from scattering in the disk while allowing near-infrared photons to reach the disk.

evidence.quote: A model geometrically reminiscent of a dusty disk wind with small micron to sub-micron-sized grains elevated above the disk can reproduce the optical effect seen in the observations. The mass in the obscuring component of the wind has been constrained to $1\times10^{-9} M_{\odot} \leq M \leq 5\times10^{-8} M_{\odot}$

In the I band, the disk is visible for a wind-dust mass of the wind foot $1\times10^{-9} M_{\odot}$ and disappears as the mass increases above $1\times10^{-8} M_{\odot}$. The disk remains visible in the H band until $5\times10^{-8} M_{\odot}$.

claims.hypothesis: The dusty disk wind in RY Tau is driven by a magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) mechanism rather than photo-evaporation (PE) or being an infalling envelope / jet-carved outflow cavity.
claims.experiment: Compared the observed horn geometry, dark wedges, inner disk properties (10 AU mm cavity, inner dust ring from 0.21 AU), and derived wind mass-loss rate (~1e-8 M_sun/yr) with theoretical MHD and PE wind simulations and expected wind-to-accretion ratios.
claims.result: The derived mass-loss rate (~1e-8 M_sun/yr) matches MHD predictions (2.22e-8 to 2.1e-7 M_sun/yr from accretion rates), the ~43 deg semi-opening angle matches 1-2 um grains in MHD winds, dark wedges and symmetry disfavour an infalling envelope, and the ~10 AU cavity with inner disk dust disfavours PE winds.
claims.finding: A magneto-centrifugally driven (MHD) disk wind is the most likely scenario, although an illuminated outflow cavity carved by the jet cannot be definitively ruled out without spatially resolved gas velocity measurements.

evidence.quote: While the disk wind hypothesis is intriguing, our analysis does not yet rule out the possibility that the optically observed morphology around RY Tau comes from an outflow cavity as a result of the jet.
While an illuminate dust cavity cannot be ruled out without measurements of the gas velocity, we argue that a magnetically launched disk wind is the most likely scenario.

why_this_data.value: Combining optical (SPHERE/ZIMPOL I band) and near-infrared (SPHERE/IRDIS H band) scattered light polarimetry with sub-millimetre (ALMA Band 6) continuum imaging allows comparison of the disk geometry with the wavelength-dependent shadowing and horn structures above the disk.

evidence.quote: By combining archival observations by SPHERE/ZIMPOL (Zurich IMaging POLarimeter; (cite: Beuzit2019; Schmid2018)), sub-millimetre observations by Atacama Large Millimetre Array (ALMA), and newly acquired near-infrared observations by SPHERE/IRDIS (Infra-Red Dual-band Imager and Spectrograph; (cite: Dohlen2008)), we discuss the possible scattered light detection of the RY Tau disk wind.

why_this_method.value: Monte Carlo radiative transfer modelling with MCMax3D allows testing whether a simple geometric model of elevated dust grains in a wind can reproduce both the SED and the synthetic scattered light images in I and H bands.

evidence.quote: We used Monte Carlo radiative transfer modelling *MCMax3D* to create comparable synthetic observations that test the effect of a dusty wind on the optical effect in the observations.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Infalling protostellar envelope (as proposed by Garufi et al. 2019): disfavoured because the H-band image shows dark wedges separating the disk from the horns and a symmetric horn structure, whereas infalling envelope material would not produce dark wedges and is expected to be asymmetric.

evidence.quote: If the elevated material is remains of the protostellar envelope, lit by the star, one would expect there to be no wedges between the disk and the envelope.

The close to symmetric horn structure in the observations of RY Tau, the opening angle and the presence of the dark wedges between the disk and the horns, all become strong indicators that the material observed above the disk is launched from the disk, rather than material falling onto the disk.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Photo-evaporative (PE) disk wind: disfavoured because PE models require large inner cleared cavities (20-30 AU) to maximize efficiency and still predict weak scattered light signals below SPHERE/IRDIS noise, whereas RY Tau has a smaller (~10 AU) mm cavity containing inner dust down to 0.21 AU.

evidence.quote: However, the cavity in the disk of RY Tau in millimetre continuum is $\sim 10$ AU, that is to say smaller than in the best case assumed for the PE model. This means that the signal of a PE wind would likely be even lower than predicted by (cite: 2022A&A...657A..69F) in the case of RY Tau.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Outflow cavity carved by the jet in a remnant envelope: considered as an alternative that cannot yet be completely ruled out without spatially resolved gas-velocity data.

evidence.quote: While the disk wind hypothesis is intriguing, our analysis does not yet rule out the possibility that the optically observed morphology around RY Tau comes from an outflow cavity as a result of the jet.

limitations_admitted.value: The Gaia EDR3 parallax quality is not optimal due to surrounding nebulosity, so the Hipparcos distance (133 pc) is used instead.

evidence.quote: The quality of the parallax, however, is not optimal due to surrounding associated nebulosity.

limitations_admitted.value: The disk scale height could not be estimated directly from the observations and was fixed based on literature radiative transfer modelling.

evidence.quote: Radiative-transfer modelling from (cite: 2013ApJ...772..145T) shows that a scale height of 5AU at a radius of 50AU matches their observations and we, not being able to estimate the scale height from our observations, chose a similar scale height and a modest flaring $\beta=1.14$.

limitations_admitted.value: In the radiative transfer model, the 10 micron silicate emission feature is weaker and less strongly peaked than in the Spitzer observations, and is dominated by the wind rather than the inner disk.

evidence.quote: In our model, however, the silicate feature is weaker than that of the observations by *SPITZER* and not as strongly peaked.

limitations_admitted.value: The synthetic H-band model images contain numerical noise spots caused by low photon statistics from stray photons scattering in the extended outer disk region.

evidence.quote: The final models contain some numerical noise in the H band images coming from stray photons that make it through the disk and scatter in the introduced outer disk region (see Fig. 4). The appearance of these spots is due to low photon statistics in this region.

limitations_admitted.value: No spatially resolved gas-velocity data are available to definitively rule out an illuminated jet-carved outflow cavity.

evidence.quote: However, no spatially resolved gas-velocity data available for RY Tau show any similar structures. While the disk wind hypothesis is intriguing, our analysis does not yet rule out the possibility that the optically observed morphology around RY Tau comes from an outflow cavity as a result of the jet.

referee_caveats_inferred: The disk wind model is purely geometric and ad hoc rather than self-consistently hydrodynamical, and the exact cone angles for the wind foot and wind top are not tabulated in the parameter table.
The gas-to-dust ratio in the wind is assumed to be 100; if grain growth and settling reduce dust entrainment, the actual gas mass-loss rate could be much higher.
The 10 micron silicate feature in the model does not match the strength and sharp peak of the Spitzer spectrum.

missing_for_reproduction: Exact geometric opening angles and vertical height parameters of the cone-shaped wind foot and wind top in MCMax3D
MCMax3D input parameter files and stellar spectrum template used
Exact contour/intensity level used for the ellipse fit to the ALMA 1.3 mm continuum image
ESO program ID for the SPHERE/IRDIS observations and ALMA project ID in the text
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: Small (<5 GB): one epoch of SPHERE/IRDIS DPI observations (17 polarimetric cycles) plus already-reduced archival SPHERE/ZIMPOL and ALMA continuum FITS images.
reproducibility.score_reason: The SPHERE/IRDIS reduction uses the public IRDAP pipeline with clearly stated exposure parameters, the horn angle measurement algorithm is described step-by-step, and most MCMax3D disk/wind parameters and SED photometry are tabulated. However, the exact cone angles for the two wind zones in MCMax3D are not explicitly listed in the table, and MCMax3D itself is not a publicly open-source code.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: ALMA plays only a minor supporting role via a previously published continuum image, and the core radiative transfer modelling relies on MCMax3D with partially unspecified wind-cone geometry parameters.
